chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
title: Demanding extra doubles for Broadway shows
summary: Crawford discusses Ernie Royal and Frank West taking Broadway shows and the doubles pay he demanded for percussion.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: I don't play now, but in case I do get a call for a job or a show, I'll take it. See, Ernie Royal, the trumpet player, Frank West, the tenor saxophone player, they told me sometime ago that they never would take a Broadway musical again. Says, they don't play music. Who did I look up and see grabbing shows and anything they could get? Ernie Royal and Frank West. And I told them about it. I say, I thought you were not going to play any more Broadway musicals.

"Oh, man, this is too good." And Ernie told a lie, talking about -- he's not in the band, he was one of them, writer talking about they were paying him four doubles. Four doubles, and he only played a trumpet.

I'm the one that was getting the doubles, because I was playing drums, tympany, whatnot, even though they had the percussionists in there. But I'd have to go over sometime and hit a note. If I hit one, got to pay me. I wouldn't take that show unless they paid me well, with two doubles at the most -- I mean, at the least. Two doubles you got to give me, on top of my union salary. Yes, sir. I wouldn't take a Broadway show.
[Ernie Lawrence] spoiled me. Didn't I tell you about me marching in the march on Washington, with --
Oh, yeah, you mentioned that, but we're going to get to that just a little bit later.
Yeah, we got to fill this thing out here.
